title: Your weekly rule
hookLine: write your week on one page; Benedict spreads the psalms over a week and calls his Rule a little rule for beginners
tomorrow: a rabbi was ordered to break his own calendar. did he obey?

lines: ALL THE PSALMS IN ONE DAY?
LET US MANAGE IT IN A WEEK.
cards: A first weekly plan can look like a wall of colored blocks, every hour spoken for. Saint Benedict, writing his Rule for monks, had a heroic standard to measure against.
The old monks, he writes, were said to sing the full hundred and fifty psalms in a single day. He doesn't ask that of his monks.
He spreads the psalms over the whole week, and says: let us, lukewarm as we are, manage it in a week.

teach.b: That line opens up the whole Rule of Saint Benedict. Near its end he calls it a little rule written for beginners. It sets a rhythm, not a feat: prayer at fixed hours, work with the hands, set times for reading.
Idleness, he writes, is the enemy of the soul, so the week has a shape. But he keeps making room inside it. Weak brothers get work that won't crush them.
The old and the young are treated gently.

teach.h: ROOM FOR THE WEAK AND THE STRONG.
teach.b: And the abbot is told to arrange everything so the strong still have something to reach for and the weak don't run away. In Christian monastic life, a rule, regula in Latin, isn't a list of punishments.

teach.h: REGULA: A FRAME TO GROW ALONG.
teach.b: It's a frame a life can grow along. Benedictine monks and nuns still live by this one, and laypeople called oblates follow it outside the cloister. And notice the unit Benedict chose.
The week. Over seven days everything gets its turn: the psalms, the work, the reading. That's what a weekly rule can be.
One page: your rest day, your service, your people, your outdoors, your study, your silence, your review, your screen-free stretch, your play, each with its day. Not everything every day.

how: Benedictine monks and nuns live by the Rule of Saint Benedict, with the psalms prayed across each week at fixed hours; oblates adapt it to ordinary lives. People writing their own weekly rule often fit it on one page, one line per day.

o: a list of rules you're never allowed to break
a strict schedule that tracks every hour
your week on one page, each practice on its day

p: all the psalms in a single day

s: Benedict asked his monks to sing every psalm each day
he spread them over a week, and called his own monks lukewarm for needing to.
Benedict called his Rule a little rule for beginners
he wrote it for beginners, with room for the weak, the old and the young.

games.q: you've written your weekly rule, and every day has five practices on it. what would Benedict's way suggest?
o: spread them out: everything in its week, not everything every day.
keep it full: a rule only counts as practice if it's hard.
drop the page and decide each morning what feels right.
games.why: Benedict spread the psalms the old monks sang in a day across a whole week, and built room for the weak into the Rule.

practice: Take a sheet of paper and draw seven short lines, one for each day. Write your rest day in first, then the longer practices, one per line, wherever they fit. Leave at least one line nearly empty.

wordCard.voice: Your weekly rule: your week on one page, each practice on its day, built the way Benedict built his, for a beginner.

orig.note: Latin: a rule, a measuring rod. The word in the title of Benedict's Rule.

carryVoice: Keep this one: my week, built for a beginner, with the psalms spread out the way Benedict spread them. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Rule of Saint Benedict, ch. 18 (the full Psalter of a hundred and fifty psalms each week; the fathers did it in a day, we lukewarm ones in a week)

Rule of Saint Benedict, ch. 48 (idleness is the enemy of the soul; work suited to the weak), ch. 37 (the old and the young), ch. 64 (the strong have something to strive for, the weak do not run away), ch. 73 (a little rule for beginners)
